clinicalPearls: Caused by brevetoxins, lipid-soluble polyether toxins produced by the dinoflagellate Karenia brevis responsible for Florida-type and Gulf of Mexico red tides, accumulated in filter-feeding shellfish.
Characteristic feature is reversal of temperature sensation, in which cold objects feel burning hot and hot objects feel cold, alongside circumoral and distal paraesthesiae.

Brevetoxins bind voltage-gated sodium channels and hold them open, causing persistent neuronal and muscle depolarisation, in contrast to the channel-blocking saxitoxins of paralytic shellfish poisoning.
Illness combines gastrointestinal symptoms with sensory neurological features, ataxia, vertigo and myalgia, but unlike paralytic poisoning life-threatening flaccid paralysis is rare.

Aerosolised brevetoxin from surf and sea spray during a red tide causes a distinct inhalational syndrome of cough, wheeze, rhinorrhoea and eye irritation, especially troublesome in people with asthma.
The toxin is heat-stable so contaminated shellfish remain hazardous after cooking, and affected shellfish look and taste normal.
Diagnosis is clinical and epidemiological, confirmed by brevetoxin assay of shellfish or body fluids at reference laboratories; management is supportive with no specific antidote.
Symptoms usually resolve within a few days, and the reported case-fatality is very low compared with paralytic shellfish poisoning.
reference.pathophysiology: Neurotoxic shellfish poisoning is produced by brevetoxins, a family of lipophilic cyclic polyether neurotoxins elaborated by the marine dinoflagellate Karenia brevis, whose proliferation generates the characteristic red tides. Filter-feeding bivalves concentrate the toxin, which is also released into sea-spray aerosols when wave action lyses the organisms. Brevetoxins bind with high affinity to a specific receptor site on voltage-gated sodium channels of excitable membranes, shifting their activation to more negative potentials and inhibiting inactivation. The channels therefore remain persistently open, causing repetitive firing, sustained depolarisation and enhanced neurotransmitter release across sensory nerves, motor nerves and autonomic fibres. This mechanism, the opposite of the sodium-channel blockade caused by saxitoxin in paralytic shellfish poisoning, explains the prominent sensory disturbances including paradoxical temperature reversal, paraesthesiae and myalgia, together with gastrointestinal and mild motor features. When inhaled, the same channel activation on airway sensory nerves and smooth muscle provokes bronchoconstriction, cough and mucosal irritation. Because the toxins are heat-stable and lipid-soluble, cooking does not detoxify contaminated shellfish.
additionalDifferentials: Paralytic shellfish poisoning (saxitoxin) with more severe paralysis
Ciguatera fish poisoning, which also causes temperature-sensation reversal and paraesthesiae
Acute asthma or reactive airways from another trigger in the inhalational form
Anxiety or hyperventilation syndrome producing paraesthesiae
additionalInvestigations: Brevetoxin detection in implicated shellfish and in serum or urine at a reference laboratory
Pulse oximetry, peak flow or spirometry in patients with inhalational or respiratory symptoms
Chest radiograph if lower-respiratory involvement or aspiration is suspected
Serum electrolytes and renal function to guide fluid and supportive management
Electrocardiogram and cardiac monitoring in patients with autonomic symptoms
Neurological examination documenting sensory reversal, ataxia and reflexes
Environmental and public-health confirmation of a concurrent Karenia brevis bloom
redFlags: Reversal of hot and cold sensation after a shellfish meal or coastal exposure
Bronchospasm, severe wheeze or respiratory distress in the inhalational form
Ataxia, vertigo or difficulty with coordinated movement
Marked bradycardia or other autonomic disturbance
Symptoms in a person with pre-existing asthma or chronic lung disease
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally excellent, with most patients recovering fully within a few days and deaths being exceptionally rare. Inhalational symptoms settle once exposure to the aerosol ceases, although those with asthma may have a more troublesome course.
pitfalls: Confusing it with the more dangerous paralytic shellfish poisoning and either over- or under-treating
Mistaking the inhalational syndrome for ordinary asthma or an allergic reaction and missing the red-tide link
Assuming cooking renders contaminated shellfish safe, as brevetoxins are heat-stable
Discounting temperature-sensation reversal as a functional complaint
Overlooking vulnerable patients with chronic respiratory disease exposed to sea-spray aerosol
references: Marine biotoxin and harmful-algal-bloom guidance documents
